(CNN) -- The bodies of young elephants covered in the brown dirt of dried-up wells tell a heartrending story. A baby elephant in the Gourma region of central Mali had been trapped in a well for three days. Reaching desperately for drops of water, they had lowered their trunks, toppled in, remained trapped and died in Mali's scorching heat. The "last desert elephants in West Africa" have "adapted to survive in the harsh conditions" they face, Save the Elephants said Monday. But now, the group says, conditions have gone from bad to worse, and they are living "on the margin of what is ecologically viable." Save the Elephants distributed new pictures Monday that depict the devastating drought and the struggle for survival in Mali, one of the poorest nations in the world. "Six elephants have already been found dead," the group wrote in a news release accompanying the photos. "Four others, including three calves, were recently extracted from a shallow well into which they had fallen when searching for water. Only the largest survived." The youngest are in the most danger, since their smaller trunks can't reach deep into the few remaining wells, the group said. The worst drought in 26 years is threatening the existence of the "last desert elephants in West Africa," the northernmost herds in the continent, Save the Elephants said. The animals, now numbering only about 350 to 450, have been called "the last elephants of Timbuktu," said Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants. But they're south of Timbuktu, Wall told CNN in a phone interview from Bamako, Mali. "We tend to refer to them as 'the last Sahelian elephants.' "  See a map of Mali » . Each year, the elephants trek farther on the fringes of the Sahara to find water. They have the longest migration route of any in the continent, traveling "in a counterclockwise circle" of about 700 kilometers (435 miles), Save the Elephants said. The images are signs of the crisis gripping the northwest African nation. The U.N. Development Programme ranks Mali near the bottom of its Human Development Index. It cites a 56 percent poverty rate in the country, with nearly a third of the population unlikely to live past age 40, and an illiteracy rate of 77 percent. The World Food Programme says the majority of infant deaths in Mali are due to malnutrition. The drought, combined with soaring temperatures, has also led to deaths of cattle, Save the Elephants said. "The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards." In areas where the elephants live and search for water, "the normal peaceful coexistence between the elephants and herdsmen is starting to break down and giving way to conflict over access to water," Wall said. There is some hope for the weeks and months ahead. "We're hoping the rains start in June, and that will allow the elephants to start drinking out of shallow ponds until the really heavy rains begin" in July or August, Wall said. But "urgent action" is needed in the interim "to secure water for the elephants," Wall's group said in its news release. Save the Elephants, which focuses on helping elephant populations worldwide, said it has partnered with a foundation and the Mali government in its fundraising appeal.

In the arid heart of West Africa lies **The Gourma**, a vast and rugged expanse of the Sahel spanning parts of Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. This unforgiving landscape is home to one of the most resilient natural wonders on Earth: the northernmost population of African elephants. Adapted to extreme heat and scarce water, **The Gourma** elephants embark on a colossal annual migration of over 300 miles—the longest known elephant migration route in the world. 

Despite their remarkable endurance, these gentle giants face unprecedented threats from habitat degradation, climate change, and poaching. Protecting a herd scattered across tens of thousands of square miles of remote desert has historically been an overwhelming challenge for rangers and conservationists.

Today, however, a new ally has joined the fight: artificial intelligence. 

Researchers and conservation groups are deploying cutting-edge **CNN** (Convolutional Neural Network) technology to monitor and protect the herd. By analyzing massive streams of visual data collected from satellite imagery, aerial drones, and remote camera traps, computer vision models built on **CNN** architectures can perform tasks that were once impossible for human teams working alone.

A modern **CNN** is uniquely suited for this work due to its ability to process complex visual spatial hierarchies. In practice, the system can instantly scan thousands of aerial photos of **The Gourma**, automatically detecting and counting individual elephants even when they are partially hidden beneath sparse desert canopy. Beyond simple tracking, specialized **CNN** algorithms can distinguish subtle visual patterns to identify individual animals, monitor their body condition, and map their migration routes in real time as water holes dry up.

Furthermore, these AI vision models serve as an automated defense network against illegal poaching. If a camera trap or drone captures night-vision footage showing unauthorized vehicles or armed individuals entering protected corridors, the **CNN** detects the threat instantly and triggers an alert for local ranger units.

The synthesis of advanced machine learning and field conservation offers a powerful beacon of hope. Through the vigilant eye of the **CNN**, technology is bridging the gap between human capabilities and the immense scale of the desert, helping to ensure that the ancient trek across **The Gourma** continues for generations to come.

In the remote Gourma region of Mali, a catastrophic and prolonged drought—exacerbated by the worsening climate crisis—is drying up the region's few remaining water sources. The crisis is pushing the world’s northernmost herd of desert-adapted elephants to the very brink of extinction.

Fewer than 300 of these rare creatures remain. For centuries, the Gourma elephants have survived in temperatures routinely exceeding 122°F (50°C), performing a epic, 370-mile annual migration—the longest recorded journey of any African elephant population—in a desperate search for food and water. 

Now, that ancient cycle of survival is breaking down.

Vital oases, such as Lake Banzena, which historically provided a lifeline during the dry season, have transformed into cracked, sun-baked mud basins. As the water vanishes, the herd is facing a harrowing reality: dehydration, starvation, and intensified conflict with local human populations who are equally desperate for resources.

### 'Beyond the edge of endurance'

Conservationists warning of an impending ecological tragedy say the speed of the environmental collapse is outstripping the elephants' ability to adapt.

"We are witnessing an unprecedented climate crisis unfolding in real-time in the Sahel," said Dr. Iain Douglas-Hamilton, founder of Save the Elephants. "These elephants are an extraordinary testament to life's resilience—they have adapted over centuries to survive in one of the harshest environments on Earth. But the sheer speed and intensity of this drought are pushing them beyond the edge of human, and animal, endurance."

The physical toll on the herd is becoming increasingly visible. Field researchers report seeing emaciated mothers unable to produce milk, leading to a devastating rise in calf mortality. 

"When the seasonal water points dry up months earlier than expected, the young and the elderly are the first to fall," a senior field biologist with Save the Elephants told CNN. "It is a heartbreaking scene. You see matriarchs desperately digging into dry riverbeds with their tusks, searching for hidden moisture, while exhausted calves collapse beside them. There is simply no water left to give them."

### A double-threat: Climate and conflict

The environmental disaster is compounded by human factors. As rainfall dwindles, nomadic Fulani herders are driven toward the same shrinking mud holes to keep their cattle alive. This competition for a few gallons of muddy water often leads to tragic encounters, with stress-maddened elephants clashing with pastoralists.

Adding to the complexity is Mali’s volatile security situation. The region has been gripped by political instability and insurgent activity for over a decade, making anti-poaching patrols and emergency conservation logistics extremely hazardous. 

Despite the perils, local ranger teams and international organizations are attempting emergency interventions, including digging deep boreholes and trucking in water to key locations along the elephants' migration corridor. But these are temporary bandages on a rapidly expanding wound.

### A race against time

The loss of the Gourma elephants would represent not just a tragic end to a unique population, but the destruction of an irreplaceable evolutionary marvel. Unlike their savanna cousins, these desert elephants have longer legs and broader feet, physical adaptations specifically suited for traversing deep sand across vast distances.

Save the Elephants and its local partners are urgently calling for expanded international support, climate-adaptation funding, and secure water management infrastructure for both the local communities and the wildlife.

"If we lose the Gourma elephants, we don't just lose a herd—we erase a genetic miracle," Douglas-Hamilton urged. "They are the guardians of the desert. Saving them requires an immediate, coordinated global effort before the dust settles on their final migration."

**Fading Footprints: Severe Drought Threatens Mali’s Rare Desert Elephants**

**BAMAKO, Mali** — In the scorching expanse of northern Mali, one of the world’s most resilient animal populations is reaching a dangerous breaking point. 

Mali’s rare desert-adapted elephants—famous for undertaking the longest annual migration of any elephant population on Earth—are facing an existential crisis as record-breaking heat and prolonged drought dry up their last remaining water sources in the Sahel.

Fewer than 350 of these unique giants remain in the Gourma region, a vast expanse south of Timbuktu. Over centuries, these elephants have adapted to the harsh environment, traveling a 350-mile (600-kilometer) loop through Mali and into neighboring Burkina Faso to find food and water. 

However, climate change is altering the region's delicate balance faster than the herds can adapt.

### A Water Basin Turned to Dust

Temperatures in the Gourma region have routinely exceeded 45°C (113°F) during the dry season, accelerating the evaporation of vital seasonal lakes. Lake Banzena, historically the crucial late-dry-season refuge for the herd, has frequently dried up entirely, leaving behind cracked, dusty earth.

"The situation is heartbreaking," said Amadou Diallo, a local community scout who works with regional conservation groups. "The elephants arrive at traditional water sites after traveling hundreds of kilometers through the desert, only to find empty sand. We are seeing exhausted mothers unable to produce milk, and young calves simply collapsing from dehydration."

As natural water points disappear, desperate elephants are entering human settlements in search of water. They are increasingly raiding community wells, stepping into cattle troughs, and destroying crops. This has sparked unprecedented conflict with local pastoralist communities, who are themselves suffering from the same devastating drought.

### A Compound Crisis: Climate and Conflict

The environmental disaster comes on top of years of political instability in the region. Since 2012, armed conflict and insecurity in northern and central Mali have made large-scale conservation efforts extremely dangerous. 

A decade ago, ivory poachers exploited the lawlessness, wiping out nearly 20% of the herd in a matter of years. While community-led conservation initiatives—such as the Mali Elephant Project—managed to curb poaching by employing local youths as "eco-guards," climate change has now eclipsed human violence as the single greatest threat to the species' survival.

"Poaching was a crisis of human greed, which we could fight with patrols and community agreements," said a wildlife researcher familiar with the region, speaking on condition of anonymity due to security concerns. "Drought is an environmental crisis. You cannot patrol against a dry sky."

### The Race to Save the Herd

The loss of Mali’s desert elephants would be a devastating blow to global biodiversity. They are one of only two adapted desert elephant populations left in the world—the other being in Namibia—and represent Africa's northernmost elephant population. 

Conservationists are racing against time to implement emergency measures. Efforts are underway to deepen existing boreholes, build solar-powered water pumps dedicated specifically to wildlife, and negotiate water-sharing agreements between elephant herds and local cattle herders.

However, funding and access remain major obstacles due to the security situation in Mali. 

Without urgent international support and sustained rainfall, experts warn that this iconic herd—a testament to nature's ability to survive in the planet's harshest conditions—could vanish within a generation.

The Sahelian elephants—the northernmost elephant herd in Africa—are caught in a deadly convergence of climate change, historic drought, and regional instability.

To survive in the harsh, sub-Saharan climate of the Gourma region, this rare population of roughly 300 elephants undertakes an extraordinary annual journey. Spanning over 700 kilometers, their circular migration path across Mali and near the border of Burkina Faso is the longest recorded migration of any elephant population on Earth. For centuries, the herd has successfully navigated this grueling trek, moving constantly from one ephemeral waterhole to the next.

However, as global temperatures soar and rainfall becomes increasingly erratic, the ancient survival strategies of the herd are failing.

### **Fatal Traps in the Sand**

With traditional lakes and seasonal ponds drying up months ahead of schedule, the elephants are driven by sheer desperation toward human settlements. Local pastoralists, faced with their own acute water shortages, have hand-dug deep, narrow wells to tap into the receding water table. 

These wells have become death traps for the herd's youngest members. Driven by extreme thirst, thirsty elephant calves often crowd around the narrow openings, leading to tragic accidents where baby elephants lose their footing and plunge into the deep pits. Unable to climb out in the stifling heat, many perish before rescue teams or local villagers can pull them to safety. 

"These elephants are living on the absolute ecological edge," says Dr. Jake Wall, a leading elephant researcher and conservationist who has spent years tracking the Gourma herd. "When the water vanishes, the herd's social fabric comes under intense pressure. Seeing a calf trapped in a well is devastating, but it is a symptom of a much larger ecosystem collapse. The water is simply gone, and the stress on these mothers and their young is unprecedented."

Wall notes that the loss of even a single calf is a devastating blow to a population already so reduced in size. "This is a unique population that has adapted to one of the harshest environments on Earth. If we lose the young, we lose the future of the entire herd," Wall added.

### **A Tragedy Set Against a Human Crisis**

The environmental disaster confronting the Sahelian elephants cannot be separated from the socio-economic crisis gripping Mali. The West African nation consistently ranks near the bottom of the United Nations Human Development Index (HDI), currently standing at 186 out of 191 countries and territories. 

Widespread poverty, high rates of food insecurity, and minimal infrastructure mean that local human populations are engaged in their own desperate struggle for daily survival. Climate change has intensified competition between nomadic herders and wildlife for shrinking pastureland and precious water resources.

Compounding the crisis is the persistent political volatility and armed conflict that has plagued northern and central Mali for over a decade. Anti-poaching patrols and research teams face constant security threats, severely limiting their ability to monitor the elephants, secure water points, or assist calves trapped in wells.

### **A Race Against Time**

Despite the daunting challenges, a coalition of international conservation groups and local community leaders are striving to implement solutions. Efforts are underway to build elephant-friendly water troughs that prevent calves from falling in, alongside initiatives that engage local communities in peaceful co-existence strategies.

Yet, as the dry season lengthens each year, time is rapidly running out for Africa’s desert wanderers. Without sustained international support, climate mitigation, and regional stability, the extraordinary 700-kilometer trek of the Sahelian elephants may soon come to a permanent end.

**A Fight for Survival: Drought and Conflict Push West Africa’s Desert Elephants to the Brink**

**By Stephane Dujarric and Eleni Giokos, CNN**
**Updated 11:42 AM EDT, October 24, 2023**

**(CNN) —** Under a blistering Sahelian sun, the last surviving herd of West Africa’s desert-adapted elephants is embarking on a desperate march. 

Driven by record-breaking droughts, the elephants of Mali’s Gourma region are tracking ancient migration routes in search of water. But as climate change shrinks the region’s vital lakes into dusty, cracked bowls, these majestic giants are colliding head-on with human communities equally desperate for survival.

The result is an escalating environmental and humanitarian crisis, where climate change, resource scarcity, and human-wildlife conflict threaten to erase one of the planet’s most unique animal populations.

### A Migration Route Built on Scarcity

The Gourma elephants are legendary. Numbering around 300 to 350 individuals, they execute the longest annual migration route of any elephant population on Earth—a grueling 300-mile circuit through the harsh, arid landscapes of Mali and neighboring Burkina Faso. 

For centuries, this herd has survived temperatures exceeding 110°F (43°C) by moving between seasonal water holes. However, extreme weather patterns driven by global climate change have shattered this delicate balance. According to the United Nations, the Sahel region is warming at 1.5 times the global average.

Key sanctuaries, such as Lake Banzena—a critical watering point during the brutal dry season—have completely dried up in recent years due to prolonged drought and over-extraction by local livestock herders.

"When Lake Banzena dried up, it was a preview of the apocalypse," says Dr. Susan Canney, Director of the Mali Elephant Project. "Elephants were dying of heatstroke and dehydration. Today, they are forced to search for water near human settlements, bringing them into direct confrontation with local populations."

### Caught in the Crossfire

As natural water sources vanish, the elephants wander into villages, smashing communal wells, destroying irrigation infrastructure, and trampling crops that feed local families. 

For the farmers and nomadic herders of the Gourma—who are already grappling with extreme poverty and food insecurity—an elephant invasion can mean total economic ruin. 

"We respect the elephants; they have always been part of our land," says Amadou Diallo, a pastoralist near the town of Douentza. "But when a herd comes to your farm, a year of food is gone in ten minutes. When your children are hungry, you view the animals as a threat, not a national treasure."

The desperation has sparked dangerous retaliatory actions. Villagers, attempting to protect their livelihoods, have used fire, poison, and firearms to drive the herds away. The tension is compounded by the shadow of illegal poaching, as criminal networks exploit the chaos and lack of local security to harvest ivory.

### The Double Crisis: Climate and Conflict

What makes the Gourma crisis uniquely complex is the security landscape. Mali has been gripped by political instability, military coups, and a violent jihadist insurgency that has swept across the Sahel since 2012. 

The conflict has severely restricted the ability of park rangers and international conservation groups to operate safely on the ground. In many areas, militant groups control the land, leaving conservationists unable to monitor the herd or assist local communities with mitigation strategies.

"This is an environmental crisis wrapped in a geopolitical crisis," says Ousmane Traoré, an environmental policy expert at the University of Bamako. "You cannot solve the human-wildlife conflict without addressing the insecurity. Park rangers cannot protect elephants when they themselves are targets for armed groups."

### Searching for Solutions

Despite the formidable obstacles, grassroots efforts offer a glimmer of hope. 

The Mali Elephant Project has been working directly with local communities to establish "eco-guards"—young locals trained to manage natural resources and herd cattle away from key elephant habitats. By creating designated water zones for livestock and others for wildlife, community leaders have successfully reduced clashes in specific corridors.

Furthermore, efforts are underway to drill deeper, solar-powered boreholes that can provide sustainable water sources for both villagers and wildlife, eliminating the need to compete for the same drying ponds.

However, conservationists warn that time is running out. Without urgent international intervention, funding, and climate mitigation, West Africa's last desert elephants could disappear within a generation.

"If we lose the Gourma elephants, we don't just lose a species—we lose an entire ecosystem's resilience," warns Dr. Canney. "They are the canary in the coal mine for the Sahel. What happens to them today will happen to the human population tomorrow."

***

*CNN’s Stephanie Busari contributed to this report from Lagos, Nigeria.*

# The Dying Giants of the Sahara: How the Worst Drought in a Generation is Erasing Timbuktu’s Last Elephants

The air in the Gourma region of Mali does not move; it bakes. Beneath a white-hot sky where temperatures routinely surge past 50 degrees Celsius (122°F), the earth has cracked into a mosaic of dry dust and broken promises. 

In this unforgiving expanse—stretching south of the legendary ancient city of Timbuktu—a heartbroken mother elephant stands over the slumped body of her calf. She uses her trunk to gently nudge the young creature, coaxing it to stand, to take one more step toward a waterhole she remembers from her youth. But the calf does not move. The waterhole no longer exists. And the mother’s milk ran dry days ago.

This is the agonizing reality unfolding at the edge of the Sahara. Gripped by the worst drought in 26 years, the last desert-adapted elephants of Timbuktu are marching toward the brink of absolute extinction. 

### The Miraculous Monarchs of the Sand

To understand the tragedy unfolding today, one must understand the sheer miracle of these animals. The Gourma elephants are the northernmost herd on the African continent, a unique population of roughly 300 to 400 individuals who have achieved the impossible for millennia: surviving in the desert.

To survive the hyper-arid environment, these gentle giants evolved a extraordinary lifestyle. They undertake a epic, 300-mile circular migration every year—the longest recorded migration route of any elephant population on Earth. Led by ancient matriarchs who carry the spatial memory of secret oases passed down through generations, the herd traverses vast swathes of sand, scrubland, and rocky plateaus in a delicate, life-or-death dance with the seasons.

They are lighter, longer-legged, and possess wider feet than their savanna cousins—adaptations designed to help them glide over loose sand and travel immense distances with minimal energy. They are the living ghosts of a green Sahara, a testament to nature’s resilience.

But even the most resilient creatures cannot survive without water. 

### A Landscape Transformed into a Graveyard

The Sahel has always been a place of extremes, but climate change has twisted hardship into horrors. The rainy season, once predictable, has fractured. The rains arrived late, sparse, and bitter, failing to replenish the vital pans and lakes that sustain the megafauna.

Lake Banzena, historically the crucial sanctuary where the herd gathers at the peak of the dry season to drink and bathe, has collapsed into a desolate dust bowl. What was once a shimmering oasis is now a choked expanse of hardened mud, littered with the sun-bleached bones of cattle and wildlife alike.

As the water points evaporate into mirages, the elephants’ desperate search for moisture has turned into a march of agony. Dehydration weakens the elders first, but it is the calves who suffer most acutely. Rangers and conservationists working in the region report horrifying scenes: mothers walking for days with dead calves slung over their tusks, unable to abandon them, while herds dig deep into dry riverbeds with their feet, drawing up only dust and dry stone.

"We are watching a slow-motion catastrophe," says one local conservation officer, who spoke under the condition of anonymity due to regional instability. "When an elephant dies of thirst, it does not die quickly. It falls from exhaustion, its organs fail under the heat, and its family stands over it, keening in a low frequency you can feel in your chest. It breaks your heart."

### The Triad of Doom: Heat, Conflict, and Chaos

The drought does not act in a vacuum. The plight of Timbuktu’s elephants is compounded by a devastating perfect storm of human conflict and environmental decay.

Mali has been torn by political instability, jihadist insurgencies, and civil strife for over a decade. The lawlessness has severely restricted the ability of international conservation agencies to patrol the vast area and protect the herd. 

Furthermore, as the drought dries up pastures across the Sahel, impoverished nomadic pastoralists are pushed into direct competition with the elephants. Thousands of starving livestock are brought to the few remaining water points, squeezing the elephants out. Desperate herders and desperate wildlife now fight over the last remaining drops of water in a desperate, tragic battle for survival where no one truly wins.

And then there is the dark shadow of poaching. While poaching had been brought under relative control in recent years thanks to local community protection initiatives, the desperation brought on by environmental collapse risks reopening the doors to illegal wildlife trade.

### The Last Echoes in the Dust

Elephants are creatures of deep empathy, complex social structures, and long memories. They mourn their dead. They comfort their young. They possess an intelligence that rivals our own, expressed in a quiet, majestic dignity. 

To lose the desert elephants of Timbuktu is not merely to lose a species from a checklist of biodiversity. It is to erase a living masterpiece of evolution—a distinct cultural memory of the Sahara that can never be recreated once it is gone.

If the monsoon rains fail again, experts warn that this unique population could cross a threshold of no return within a matter of months. The loss will not be quiet; it will leave a hollow, echoing silence across the dunes.

As the sun sets over the parched landscape of the Gourma, casting long, mournful shadows across the cracked earth, the remaining herd pushes forward through the dark, trusting in a matriarch whose memory is being tested by an unrecognizable world. They move forward because they must. But without urgent global intervention, rain, and peace, the footsteps of Timbuktu’s giants will soon be wiped away by the desert winds forever.
